title: Working Better with Parents
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that working well with parents starts with humility: assuming the parent loves the child more than the teacher ever can and wants the child's flourishing even more. Although a teacher may have more professional knowledge, he insists knowledge is not wisdom or love, and he argues that arrogance estranges many families from public schools. He then redefines communication as achieved only when both sides actually understand each other and know what to do next. Most parent-teacher conflict, he says, is a communication breakdown, and teachers should own their part of it instead of blaming parents and sinking into a victim mentality. He contrasts habits that push parents away (jargon, long monologues, condescension, sugarcoating) with those that build partnership (simplicity, honesty, a doctor's bedside manner, reflecting on the class from a parent's view). For hostile parents, he advises professional detachment and keeping self-worth separate from the job, letting hard encounters refine rather than burn out the teacher.
points: Stuart's starting point is humility: assume the parent loves the child more than you and wants the child's flourishing more than you do.
Communication is redefined as mutual understanding with a clear outcome, not simply talking or listening.
He argues teachers should treat every breakdown as partly their own fault, because blaming parents leaves them powerless and breeds a victim mentality.
Keeping professional identity separate from self-worth lets a teacher handle angry parents analytically instead of in fight-or-flight mode.

His practical list of things to avoid (jargon, condescension, telling only nice things) and to do (speak simply, tell the whole truth, review the class from a parent's view) makes the stance actionable.
quotes: Humility calls us to assume that the parent or guardian we are working with at any given time loves the kid more than we'll ever be able to. It calls us to assume that the parent, therefore, wants that child's long-term flourishing infinitely more than we ever can.
It's not a silver bullet, mind you, but a humble attitude disarms people and makes them believe in their gut that you're on their team because, in humility, you realize that you are.

You'll know you have communicated when, after a conversation, both parties know what they need to do or they feel better or both. You'll know you haven't communicated when, after a conversation, nothing has changed.

If I encounter an angry or offensive parent and my sense of self-worth is attached to how things go, then I'm going to fight or run to protect myself. Yet if I enter the same situation with professional detachment, I'm able to analyze it like one would a puzzle and determine how to best remedy things.
This enables action and disables the life-draining, I'm-a-victim mentality that I see killing far too many teachers. Folks, we're not victims. We're professionals.

If a parent insults you, it's generally not at all about you. It's about their own issues, their own idolatries, their own warped psyches. We'll know we've nailed this when we continue to wholeheartedly seek to serve them and their child even when they treat us horribly.
But when we leave that school building for the day, it's not as a failure. We don't haul home a load of self-recrimination. Why? Because we are not only teachers — we are people.
